### Background
In recent decades, nanoparticles (NPs) have emerged as a subject of immense importance across multiple scientific disciplines. Their applications have proliferated in various industries, including pharmaceuticals, medicine, cosmetics, construction, and electronics, making them integral to materials science [ 1 ]. The growing interest in nanoparticles is driven by their unique properties and potential for innovative applications in these fields. Nanoparticles are distinguished by their nanoscale size, typically ranging from 1 to 100 nm, which results in a high surface area-to-volume ratio, enhanced surface reactivity, and unique physicochemical properties. They also exhibit diverse morphologies, including nanotubes, nanorods, nanoconjugates, and nanowires, which differ significantly from their bulk counterparts [ 1 ].
Furthermore, metal NPs have garnered widespread attention owing to their unique properties, including anticancer, antimicrobial, and antioxidant activities, as well as distinctive physicochemical characteristics such as controlled morphology, conductivity, particle size distribution, and optical and magnetic properties [ 2 , 3 ]. Although various methods exist for synthesizing NPs, physical and chemical approaches are recognized for their energy-intensive nature, environmental toxicity, and high cost. In contrast, biosynthesis, often referred to as "green synthesis," offers an eco-friendly alternative that requires lower energy consumption and financial investment, resulting in biocompatible nanoparticles [ 4 ]. Biosynthesis employs a range of biological sources, such as plants, microbes, and algae, to produce metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional synthesis methods [ 5 ].

### Research gap
Traditionally, the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) has predominantly relied on plant and microbial bioresources. Plant-mediated approaches have utilized species such as Moringa oleifera , Azadirachta indica (Neem), Bryophyllum pinnatum , and Citrullus colocynthis , where metabolites including flavonoids, tannins, and proteins act as reducing and stabilizing agents [ 2 , 14 , 15 ]. Microbial systems, including fungi and bacteria, have also been explored for biogenic Ag-NP production, though these processes often require longer incubation periods, precise culture conditions, and post-culture processing [ 16 ].
In contrast, the use of animal-derived systems, particularly insects, remains underexplored despite their rich biochemical composition. Musca domestica L. (housefly) was selected in this study based on several practical and mechanistic considerations: its global abundance and ease of collection, minimal maintenance requirements, and the presence of diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and metabolites, capable of reducing Ag + ions and stabilizing nanoparticles [ 15 , 17 – 19 ]. The use of whole insect extract provides a complex biochemical environment that supports rapid nanoparticle formation (within 15 min) without the need for additional chemicals, highlighting a chemical-free and efficient synthesis approach.

### Experimental design, and laboratory setting
The experimental workflow comprised several sequential stages: (i) collection and taxonomic verification of houseflies, (ii) preparation of aqueous extract, (iii) biosynthesis of Ag–NPs, (iv) detailed physicochemical characterization including UV–Vis spectroscopy, FTIR, SEM, EDX, XRD, DLS, and zeta potential analysis, and (v) in vitro assessment of therapeutic potential. Each step was designed to ensure reproducibility and reliability, with triplicate measurements, multiple runs, and standardized protocols applied throughout. Statistical analysis is conducted to determine significance, compare groups, and interpret data. Laboratory setting

### Collection &amp; extract preparation of houseflies
Following a modified protocol by Jakinala et al. [ 21 ], 300 adult houseflies ( Musca domestica L.) were collected randomly in polythene bags from meat, fruit, and vegetable markets in Karachi. This exploratory approach was intended to assess the practical potential of M. domestica extract without introducing bias from laboratory-reared specimens or chemical additives. Flies were euthanized via asphyxiation, and a subset of 30 specimens was sent to the Department of Zoology, University of Karachi, for taxonomic verification. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed the species identity.
The collected flies were washed three times with ethanol and deionized water to remove surface contaminants. To preserve the natural biochemical composition, no organic solvent-based extraction (ethanol or methanol) was performed. The flies were then homogenized in deionized water, filtered through the exoskeleton using a sieve, and centrifuged at 7000 rpm for 20 min. The resulting supernatant was collected and stored at 4°C for subsequent silver nanoparticle synthesis and in vitro analyses [ 21 , 22 ].
As this study was exploratory, flies were collected randomly without controlling for gender or developmental stage. While this introduces natural variability in metabolite composition, it reflects real-world conditions and allows a practical evaluation of the extract’s utility. Future studies may employ laboratory-reared flies of defined age and gender to standardize metabolite profiles, optimize nanoparticle synthesis, and enhance reproducibility and mechanistic understanding.

### Biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles
The biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles was carried out by mixing the prepared housefly extract with a 1 mM aqueous solution of silver nitrate (AgNO 3 ) at a ratio of 1:9 (extract: AgNO 3 ). A control sample, containing distilled water instead of the extract, was prepared to account for any non-biological reduction of silver ions. The mixture was incubated in a shaking water bath at 70°C for 15 min [ 25 ]. The selected temperature and incubation time were based on preliminary optimization trials, which indicated that these conditions promoted efficient reduction of Ag + ions, as evidenced by a rapid and stable color change from colorless to reddish-brown, without compromising the stability or uniformity of the nanoparticles. The formation of Ag–NPs under these conditions is consistent with previously reported green synthesis protocols, where moderate heat accelerates the bioreduction process without denaturing the bioactive compounds in the extract [ 21 , 22 , 26 ].
Following incubation, the colloidal suspension was visually monitored for the characteristic reddish-brown color, indicating successful nanoparticle formation. The resulting Ag–NPs were stored at 4°C until further physicochemical characterization and in vitro biochemical analyses. This approach ensures reproducibility, as the standardized temperature and time conditions consistently yielded nanoparticles of comparable size and stability across replicate preparations as demonstrated in Tables 1 and 2 . The method reflects an eco-friendly and practical synthesis strategy while minimizing the need for hazardous chemicals.

### Characterization of biogenic nanoparticles
Visual investigation of nanoparticles
Formation of Ag–NPs was first confirmed visually, followed by quantitative UV–Vis spectroscopy using a BIOBASE BK-S360 spectrophotometer over 300–600 nm. Measurements were performed in triplicate across multiple days to ensure reproducibility [ 21 , 22 , 25 ]. A summary of UV–Vis absorbance runs and replicates is provided in Table 1 . Morphological analysis (SEM)
A drop of the colloidal suspension was deposited on a glass coverslip, air-dried, and observed under SEM (JSM-6380) at 35,000 × magnification [ 3 , 12 ]. Particle shapes and sizes were determined, and size distribution was calculated as σ/μ, providing insight into homogeneity [ 27 ]. To avoid confusion with DLS polydispersity index (PDI), this is reported as “size distribution from SEM.” Structural analysis (XRD)
Dried Ag-NP powder was analyzed using a Bruker D2 Phaser XRD system with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å) in Bragg–Brentano geometry (2θ = 10–80°, 1°/min). Crystal planes were assigned using JCPDS Card No. 04-0783. Crystallite sizes were calculated using the Scherrer equation [ 26 ].
where D = crystallite size, K = 0.9, λ = 1.54 nm, β = FWHM in radians, θ = Bragg angle. For the most intense peak observed at approximately 38.35° (111), the FWHM (β) was 0.151 rad. Elemental analysis (EDX)
EDX was performed on SEM-mounted samples over 0–20 keV to determine elemental composition and assess potential contaminants [ 28 ]. FTIR analysis
FTIR spectra were recorded to identify functional groups responsible for Ag + reduction and nanoparticle stabilization. Sixteen scans with a resolution of 4 cm −1 were collected over 4000–400 cm −1 [ 25 , 29 ]. A summary table of major peaks and probable functional groups is provided in Table 3 .

### In Vitro biological evaluations of biosynthesized Ag–NPs
All assays were performed at a single concentration of 500 µg/mL. Anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, DPPH radical scavenging, and H 2 O 2 scavenging activities were assessed according to previously published protocols [ 31 , 33 – 35 ]. Results were expressed as percentage inhibition or scavenging relative to respective positive and negative controls. A fixed concentration was selected to enable comparative screening across treatments under uniform conditions.
As only one concentration was tested, direct IC 50 calculation was not feasible. The single concentration was chosen to provide a preliminary assessment of therapeutic potential and to compare effects with controls (AgNO 3 and standard drugs).
Justification for single concentration use In this study, a single concentration of 500 µg/mL was employed for all biomedical assays to provide an initial assessment of the biological potential of the biosynthesized silver nanoparticles. This approach allowed for efficient screening and proof-of-concept evaluation of their activity, conserving resources while confirming that the nanoparticles exhibit measurable effects. However, it is acknowledged as a limitation, as it does not allow determination of IC 50 values or a full dose–response profile. Future studies should include multiple concentrations to establish potency and therapeutic windows more accurately.
The anti-inflammatory properties of Ag–NPs were assessed following the protocols of [ 36 ] using a protein denaturation assay. Briefly, a working albumin solution was prepared by diluting 2 mL of 100 mg/10 mL PBS stock into 28 mL PBS. For each test sample, 300 µL of working albumin solution was mixed with 400 µL of Ag–NPs solution or Diclofenac sodium as a positive control. Vehicle control tubes contained 400 µL of DMSO. The mixtures were incubated at room temperature for 10 min, followed by heating at 65°C for 15 min to induce protein denaturation, and then cooled to room temperature. ### Macroscopic and microscopic morphological characterization of Musca domestica L.
The external morphology of Musca domestica L. was examined both macroscopically and microscopically to confirm specimen identity. As shown in Fig. 1 , “Panel a” (dorsal view) revealed large red compound eyes, short aristate antennae with prominent lateral bristles, and a gray thorax marked with four longitudinal black stripes. Wings were positioned dorsally, and the tarsus comprised five tarsomeres with a pretarsus terminating in two claws. “Panel b” (lateral view) showed a single pair of functional forewings that were transparent and membranous with distinct venation, characteristic of Diptera. Three pairs of segmented legs (forelegs, midlegs, and hindlegs) were attached ventrally, each consisting of a femur, tibia, tarsus, and pretarsus. “Panel c” (dorsal oblique view) highlighted well-defined red compound eyes, folded wings, a darkly pigmented thorax with four black longitudinal stripes, a yellowish-brown abdomen with visible segmental bands, and a proboscis extending ventrally from the head capsule [ 16 , 41 ].
Magnified macroscopic external morphological views of Musca domestica L. under natural light Microscopic examination (Fig. 2 ) further confirmed these traits. “Panel a” displayed the mouthparts, including a proboscis adapted for sucking and sponging, with sclerotized components (labrum, labium, maxillary palps). “Panel b” highlighted compound eye clusters with optic nerves. “Panel c” showed a transparent membranous wing with distinct venation and a dark oval pterostigma along the leading edge. “Panel d” revealed club-shaped halteres, modified hindwings acting as gyroscopic organs. “Panel e” depicted the hindleg, longer and more robust for propulsion, while “Panel f” illustrated the midleg, thicker and blunter, with a pretarsus bearing terminal claws.

### Verification of desired colour change at 70 °C
The initial qualitative assessment of Ag-NP formation relied on observable color changes, an established preliminary indicator of nanoparticle synthesis [ 23 ]. Upon addition of Musca domestica L. extract to a colorless silver nitrate solution and incubation at 70°C in a shaking water bath, the solution gradually changed to a red-brown hue, forming a distinct brown colloid within 15 min (Fig. 3 ). This visible transformation is attributed to the reduction of Ag + ions to metallic Ag 0 nanoparticles, corroborating the formation of Ag–NPs.

### UV–Vis spectroscopy analysis
The formation of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) was further confirmed by UV–Vis spectroscopy (Fig. 4 ). The observed SPR peak at 475 nm confirms the formation of Ag–NPs and falls within the typical range of 400–500 nm reported for green-synthesized silver nanoparticles [ 25 ]. This range is attributed to surface plasmon resonance (SPR), a phenomenon arising from the collective oscillation of conduction electrons at the interface between negatively charged electrons and the positively charged metal lattice upon interaction with incident light [ 25 ].

### Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) analysis
SEM was employed to directly visualize the morphology and size distribution of the synthesized Ag–NPs (Fig. 5 ). The images revealed predominantly spherical nanoparticles with diameters ranging approximately from 70 to 82 nm. The average particle size was determined to be 76 ± 6 nm. Similar findings have been reported in several studies, including a study conducted in 2024 [ 12 ]. This observed variation of 0.0058 is described here as “size distribution from SEM”, rather than polydispersity index (PDI), since PDI is conventionally derived from dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements [ 27 ].
SEM image showing the spherical shape and uniform size distribution of Ag–NPs The DLS analysis (Sect. 3.8 ) reported a hydrodynamic diameter of 258.5 nm with a PDI of 0.371. The larger DLS value compared to SEM is expected, as DLS measures the particle plus its surrounding hydration layer and any potential aggregation in solution, whereas SEM measures dry, individual nanoparticles. These differences highlight that the Ag–NPs, while relatively uniform in their intrinsic size, may form loose aggregates in suspension, contributing to the larger hydrodynamic diameter. Similar results were observed in a 2025 study [ 3 ].

### X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis
XRD analysis was conducted to evaluate the crystalline nature and phase purity of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs (Fig. 6 ). The diffraction pattern exhibited prominent peaks at 38.1° (111), 44.3° (200), 64.4° (220), and 77.3° (311), consistent with the face-centered cubic (fcc) structure of metallic silver [ 12 ]. These reflections confirm the formation of crystalline Ag–NPs at the nanoscale. The calculated average crystallite size, using the Debye–Scherrer equation, was approximately 9.72 nm, indicating nanocrystalline properties.

### Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
The EDX spectrum (Fig. 7 ) provided a detailed elemental composition of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs. A strong peak at 3 keV confirmed the presence of silver, which accounted for 20.01% of the total mass. The relatively low silver content, compared to theoretical 100% silver, reflects the presence of stabilizing biomolecules and other elements derived from the housefly extract [ 7 ]. These capping molecules, including proteins, sugars, and phenolics, coat the nanoparticle surface and are detected by EDX, reducing the apparent silver mass fraction.
EDX spectrum showing the elemental composition of Ag–NPs with a dominant silver peak Other elements detected included C, O, Na, Mg, Al, Ca, and Au. Carbon and oxygen are expected, as they arise from organic biomolecules present in the housefly extract. Sodium and magnesium may be derived from salts or mineral components within the extract. Trace amounts of aluminum, calcium, or gold could result from environmental exposure of the flies, sample preparation, or the substrate used for SEM imaging. These findings align with previous reports of biologically synthesized nanoparticles where non-metallic residues and elemental traces are commonly observed [ 13 ].

### Biomolecule Identification via Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis (Comparative study)
The FTIR spectrum of the Musca domestica L. extract revealed characteristic absorption bands corresponding to diverse biomolecular functional groups, which were also observed in the biosynthesized Ag–NPs spectrum with notable variations (Fig. 8 a and b), summarized in Table 3 . In the extract, a broad band in the range of 3700–3200 cm −1 is attributed to O–H stretching vibrations of hydroxyl groups present in phenolics, proteins, and carbohydrates. A less intense band in the 2800–2600 cm −1 region corresponds to C–H stretching vibrations of aliphatic chains in sugars and other organic molecules [ 1 ]. The band around 1651–1631 cm −1 is assigned to C=O stretching of carbonyl groups and aromatic structures [ 3 ], while the region between 1365 and 1030 cm −1 represents C–N, C–O, and C–O–C stretching vibrations, indicating the presence of amines, alcohols, ethers, and reducing sugars [ 30 ].
FTIR spectra of a biosynthesized Ag–NPs and b Musca domestica L. extract, showing functional group variations associated with nanoparticle formation In comparison, the biosynthesized Ag–NPs spectrum retained these functional group signatures but exhibited shifts in peak positions and changes in intensity, indicating interactions between silver ions and biomolecules during nanoparticle formation. The broad O–H/N–H band around 3273 cm −1 appeared more intense and slightly shifted, suggesting enhanced hydrogen bonding and possible involvement of hydroxyl- and amine-containing compounds in nanoparticle synthesis [ 3 ]. Such changes may also be influenced by environmental factors such as pH and local ionic conditions during synthesis, which can alter hydrogen bonding and biomolecular conformation.
The bands at 1637 cm −1 and 1344 cm −1 showed slight shifts relative to the extract, indicating potential interaction of carbonyl and aromatic groups with Ag + ions. These groups may contribute to electron transfer processes required for reduction, although this cannot be conclusively establish

### Zeta size and potential
The hydrodynamic size of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs was determined by dynamic light scattering (DLS) and found to be 258.5 nm, with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.371 (Fig. 9 a). This hydrodynamic size is substantially larger than the size observed in SEM analysis (76 ± 6 nm), which represents the core metallic nanoparticles [ 43 ]. Similar findings have been reported in the literature, with [ 28 ] determining the average hydrodynamic size of Ag–NPs to be 231.8 nm. The discrepancy arises because DLS measures the effective diameter of particles in suspension, including the hydration layer and any adsorbed biomolecules from the housefly extract that act as capping agents. Furthermore, partial aggregation in aqueous media can contribute to a larger observed size in DLS measurements.
a Zeta size distribution of Ag–NPs synthesized using housefly extract, showing an average hydrodynamic size of 258.5 nm with a PDI of 0.371. b Zeta potential distribution indicating a surface charge of − 7.98 ± 5.93 mV The PDI of 0.371, while below 0.5, indicates moderate polydispersity, reflecting some size variation in the colloidal suspension [ 22 , 44 ]. In comparison, the “size distribution from SEM” suggests relatively uniform individual nanoparticles but does not account for the surrounding hydration layer or aggregation in solution. This comparison emphasizes the importance of using both imaging and hydrodynamic measurements to fully characterize nanoparticle populations.
The zeta potential of the Ag–NPs was measured at − 7.98 mV (Fig. 9 b). Although a negative value suggests some degree of electrostatic repulsion, it is relatively low compared to the ± 30 mV threshold typically considered necessary for long-term colloidal stability [ 44 ]. Therefore, the nanoparticles may possess moderate short-term stability, sufficient for the current in vitro assays, but might be prone to aggregation over extended storage or under varying physicochemical conditions. ### Therapeutic potential of biosynthesized Ag–NPs
The therapeutic potential of biosynthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) was systematically evaluated through in vitro assays, including anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, and antioxidant activities. Percentage inhibition values were calculated from triplicate (n = 3) absorbance measurements.
In the anti-inflammatory assay, Ag–NPs showed moderate inhibition of protein denaturation (21.73% ± 1.55% b ) relative to AgNO 3 (9.54% ± 1.35% c ) and the housefly extract (5.01% ± 0.85% d ), whereas Diclofenac, used as a standard, displayed the highest inhibition (36.04% ± 1.93% a ) (Table 4 ). DMSO, serving as a negative control, showed negligible activity (0.00% e ). One-way ANOVA indicated significant differences among treatments (F 4,10 = 80.58, p &lt; 0.001), and Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis confirmed that Ag–NPs’ activity was significantly greater than both AgNO 3 and the extract, but lower than Diclofenac (p &lt; 0.05). These results highlight the enhanced anti-inflammatory potential of Ag–NPs compared to ionic silver and the crude extract, likely due to nanoparticle-mediated stabilization and bioactive surface functionalization [ 9 , 33 ].

### Discussion
The biosynthesis of Ag–NPs using Musca domestica L. extract represents a complex biologically mediated redox system in which diverse insect-derived metabolites collectively govern nanoparticle formation and stabilization.
The UV–Vis spectral analysis further confirms nanoparticle formation, with an SPR peak observed at 475 nm within the typical range of 400–500 nm for green-synthesized Ag–NPs [ 25 ]. Comparable studies have reported SPR peaks at 463 nm ( Justicia adhatoda ), 488 nm ( Equisetum arvense ), and 445 nm ( Withania coagulans ), indicating that the optical response is strongly influenced by the biological source [ 25 ]. The slight red-shift observed in the present study may be attributed to biomolecule-induced changes in the local dielectric environment and mild interparticle interactions, which increase the effective particle size [ 32 ]. These findings emphasize that nanoparticle optical properties are governed not only by size but also by interfacial chemistry and surface-bound organic layers [ 34 , 46 ]. The physicochemical characteristics, including moderate dispersity (PDI = 0.385) and the discrepancy between primary particle size and hydrodynamic diameter, indicate the formation of a biomolecular corona and soft agglomeration in aqueous environments [ 3 ]. Such behavior is widely reported in green-synthesized nanoparticles and is attributed to the adsorption of organic constituents rather than actual particle growth [ 37 ]. This suggests that the nanoparticles exist as hybrid organic–inorganic systems, where surface-bound biomolecules significantly influence colloidal behavior and functionality.
The colloidal stability of the synthesized nanoparticles appears to be primarily governed by steric rather than electrostatic effects. The relatively low zeta potential, together with the increased hydrodynamic size, suggests that stabilization is achieved through a biomolecular coating that limits aggregation via physical hindrance [ 15 , 37 ]. ### Limitations of the study
While this work establishes the feasibility of using M. domestica aqueous extract for Ag–NP biosynthesis, several limitations exist:
Exploratory Design and Random Sampling Flies were collected randomly from markets without controlling for gender or age. This may introduce variability in biochemical composition. Future studies should employ lab-reared flies to standardize the extract.
Single-Concentration Bioassays In vitro assays were conducted at a single concentration, preventing IC 50 determination. Although preliminary bioactivity was demonstrated, future studies should include dose–response analyses to calculate IC 50 and fully quantify therapeutic potential.
Comparison with Solvent-Based Extracts While prior studies used ethanolic or methanolic extracts, the current work employed aqueous extraction for environmental and biocompatibility reasons. Direct side-by-side experimental comparisons with solvent-based extracts could strengthen conclusions regarding efficiency and functional equivalence.
Optimization of Synthesis Parameters Temperature and incubation time were selected based on preliminary observations, not a full factorial optimization. Future work should systematically evaluate parameters such as pH, temperature, extract-to-silver ratio, and incubation duration to refine synthesis efficiency and nanoparticle stability.
Biochemical Variability Variations in metabolite composition of houseflies may affect reproducibility. Comprehensive profiling of bioactive compounds in the extract could provide mechanistic insights and enhance consistency.

### Future directions and recommendations
Future investigations should aim for a more detailed mechanistic understanding of nanoparticle formation by isolating and characterizing the specific biomolecular fractions responsible for reduction and capping. While the present findings suggest a synergistic role of proteins, phenolics, and other metabolites, the relative contribution of each component remains unclear. Advanced analytical approaches, such as proteomic and metabolomic profiling, could identify key functional molecules and elucidate their binding interactions with metal ions, enabling more controlled and reproducible synthesis pathways.
To strengthen the biological interpretation of these findings, systematic dose–response evaluations are necessary to determine IC 50 values and establish concentration-dependent effects. This would facilitate rigorous comparison with existing nanomaterials and conventional agents, while clarifying whether observed activities are primarily nanoparticle-driven or influenced by residual ionic silver or surface-associated biomolecules.
Standardization of the biological source represents another critical requirement. Variations in metabolite composition due to age, diet, or physiological state of Musca domestica L. may significantly influence nanoparticle characteristics. The use of controlled, lab-reared specimens under defined conditions could minimize batch-to-batch variability and enhance reproducibility, a recognized limitation in bio-mediated synthesis systems.
Further studies should include cytotoxicity and biocompatibility assessments using relevant mammalian cell models to define safety profiles, which is essential if the biomedical potential of these nanoparticles is to be claimed. In parallel, stability optimization through surface engineering, such as controlled functionalization or selective purification of capping layers, may improve colloidal stability and enable more predictable interactions in biological environments.

### Conclusion
Silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) were successfully synthesized using houseflies extract as a novel bioresource via a rapid and green approach. The present study demonstrates that Musca domestica L. extract can serve as a novel and effective bioresource for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs). The nanoparticles exhibit well-defined crystalline structures, moderate colloidal stability, and surface functionalization by biomolecules, as confirmed through UV–Vis, SEM, FTIR, Zeta Potential. DLS, and XRD analyses. Mechanistic insights suggest that proteins, phenolics, and other metabolites act synergistically to reduce Ag + ions and stabilize the resulting nanoparticles, while FTIR-identified functional groups provide molecular-level justification for their potent antioxidant activity.
Functionally, the biosynthesized Ag–NPs exhibit promising anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-diabetic activities. Although ionic silver contributes to some observed effects, the surface-bound biomolecules and nanoparticle interface likely enhance overall performance, highlighting the importance of hybrid organic–inorganic structures. These findings underscore the potential of insect-mediated nanoparticle synthesis as a sustainable and versatile platform for biomedical applications.

Biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles using Musca domestica extract as a novel bioresource for therapeutic evaluation

### Background
In recent decades, nanoparticles (NPs) have emerged as a subject of immense importance across multiple scientific disciplines. Their applications have proliferated in various industries, including pharmaceuticals, medicine, cosmetics, construction, and electronics, making them integral to materials science [ 1 ]. The growing interest in nanoparticles is driven by their unique properties and potential for innovative applications in these fields. Nanoparticles are distinguished by their nanoscale size, typically ranging from 1 to 100 nm, which results in a high surface area-to-volume ratio, enhanced surface reactivity, and unique physicochemical properties. They also exhibit diverse morphologies, including nanotubes, nanorods, nanoconjugates, and nanowires, which differ significantly from their bulk counterparts [ 1 ].
Furthermore, metal NPs have garnered widespread attention owing to their unique properties, including anticancer, antimicrobial, and antioxidant activities, as well as distinctive physicochemical characteristics such as controlled morphology, conductivity, particle size distribution, and optical and magnetic properties [ 2 , 3 ]. Although various methods exist for synthesizing NPs, physical and chemical approaches are recognized for their energy-intensive nature, environmental toxicity, and high cost. In contrast, biosynthesis, often referred to as "green synthesis," offers an eco-friendly alternative that requires lower energy consumption and financial investment, resulting in biocompatible nanoparticles [ 4 ]. Biosynthesis employs a range of biological sources, such as plants, microbes, and algae, to produce metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional synthesis methods [ 5 ].

### Research gap
Traditionally, the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) has predominantly relied on plant and microbial bioresources. Plant-mediated approaches have utilized species such as Moringa oleifera , Azadirachta indica (Neem), Bryophyllum pinnatum , and Citrullus colocynthis , where metabolites including flavonoids, tannins, and proteins act as reducing and stabilizing agents [ 2 , 14 , 15 ]. Microbial systems, including fungi and bacteria, have also been explored for biogenic Ag-NP production, though these processes often require longer incubation periods, precise culture conditions, and post-culture processing [ 16 ].
In contrast, the use of animal-derived systems, particularly insects, remains underexplored despite their rich biochemical composition. Musca domestica L. (housefly) was selected in this study based on several practical and mechanistic considerations: its global abundance and ease of collection, minimal maintenance requirements, and the presence of diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and metabolites, capable of reducing Ag + ions and stabilizing nanoparticles [ 15 , 17 – 19 ]. The use of whole insect extract provides a complex biochemical environment that supports rapid nanoparticle formation (within 15 min) without the need for additional chemicals, highlighting a chemical-free and efficient synthesis approach.

### Experimental design, and laboratory setting
The experimental workflow comprised several sequential stages: (i) collection and taxonomic verification of houseflies, (ii) preparation of aqueous extract, (iii) biosynthesis of Ag–NPs, (iv) detailed physicochemical characterization including UV–Vis spectroscopy, FTIR, SEM, EDX, XRD, DLS, and zeta potential analysis, and (v) in vitro assessment of therapeutic potential. Each step was designed to ensure reproducibility and reliability, with triplicate measurements, multiple runs, and standardized protocols applied throughout. Statistical analysis is conducted to determine significance, compare groups, and interpret data. Laboratory setting

### Collection &amp; extract preparation of houseflies
Following a modified protocol by Jakinala et al. [ 21 ], 300 adult houseflies ( Musca domestica L.) were collected randomly in polythene bags from meat, fruit, and vegetable markets in Karachi. This exploratory approach was intended to assess the practical potential of M. domestica extract without introducing bias from laboratory-reared specimens or chemical additives. Flies were euthanized via asphyxiation, and a subset of 30 specimens was sent to the Department of Zoology, University of Karachi, for taxonomic verification. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed the species identity.
The collected flies were washed three times with ethanol and deionized water to remove surface contaminants. To preserve the natural biochemical composition, no organic solvent-based extraction (ethanol or methanol) was performed. The flies were then homogenized in deionized water, filtered through the exoskeleton using a sieve, and centrifuged at 7000 rpm for 20 min. The resulting supernatant was collected and stored at 4°C for subsequent silver nanoparticle synthesis and in vitro analyses [ 21 , 22 ].
As this study was exploratory, flies were collected randomly without controlling for gender or developmental stage. While this introduces natural variability in metabolite composition, it reflects real-world conditions and allows a practical evaluation of the extract’s utility. Future studies may employ laboratory-reared flies of defined age and gender to standardize metabolite profiles, optimize nanoparticle synthesis, and enhance reproducibility and mechanistic understanding.

### Biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles
The biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles was carried out by mixing the prepared housefly extract with a 1 mM aqueous solution of silver nitrate (AgNO 3 ) at a ratio of 1:9 (extract: AgNO 3 ). A control sample, containing distilled water instead of the extract, was prepared to account for any non-biological reduction of silver ions. The mixture was incubated in a shaking water bath at 70°C for 15 min [ 25 ]. The selected temperature and incubation time were based on preliminary optimization trials, which indicated that these conditions promoted efficient reduction of Ag + ions, as evidenced by a rapid and stable color change from colorless to reddish-brown, without compromising the stability or uniformity of the nanoparticles. The formation of Ag–NPs under these conditions is consistent with previously reported green synthesis protocols, where moderate heat accelerates the bioreduction process without denaturing the bioactive compounds in the extract [ 21 , 22 , 26 ].
Following incubation, the colloidal suspension was visually monitored for the characteristic reddish-brown color, indicating successful nanoparticle formation. The resulting Ag–NPs were stored at 4°C until further physicochemical characterization and in vitro biochemical analyses. This approach ensures reproducibility, as the standardized temperature and time conditions consistently yielded nanoparticles of comparable size and stability across replicate preparations as demonstrated in Tables 1 and 2 . The method reflects an eco-friendly and practical synthesis strategy while minimizing the need for hazardous chemicals.

### Characterization of biogenic nanoparticles
Visual investigation of nanoparticles
Formation of Ag–NPs was first confirmed visually, followed by quantitative UV–Vis spectroscopy using a BIOBASE BK-S360 spectrophotometer over 300–600 nm. Measurements were performed in triplicate across multiple days to ensure reproducibility [ 21 , 22 , 25 ]. A summary of UV–Vis absorbance runs and replicates is provided in Table 1 . Morphological analysis (SEM)
A drop of the colloidal suspension was deposited on a glass coverslip, air-dried, and observed under SEM (JSM-6380) at 35,000 × magnification [ 3 , 12 ]. Particle shapes and sizes were determined, and size distribution was calculated as σ/μ, providing insight into homogeneity [ 27 ]. To avoid confusion with DLS polydispersity index (PDI), this is reported as “size distribution from SEM.” Structural analysis (XRD)
Dried Ag-NP powder was analyzed using a Bruker D2 Phaser XRD system with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å) in Bragg–Brentano geometry (2θ = 10–80°, 1°/min). Crystal planes were assigned using JCPDS Card No. 04-0783. Crystallite sizes were calculated using the Scherrer equation [ 26 ].
where D = crystallite size, K = 0.9, λ = 1.54 nm, β = FWHM in radians, θ = Bragg angle. For the most intense peak observed at approximately 38.35° (111), the FWHM (β) was 0.151 rad. Elemental analysis (EDX)
EDX was performed on SEM-mounted samples over 0–20 keV to determine elemental composition and assess potential contaminants [ 28 ]. FTIR analysis
FTIR spectra were recorded to identify functional groups responsible for Ag + reduction and nanoparticle stabilization. Sixteen scans with a resolution of 4 cm −1 were collected over 4000–400 cm −1 [ 25 , 29 ]. A summary table of major peaks and probable functional groups is provided in Table 3 .

### In Vitro biological evaluations of biosynthesized Ag–NPs
All assays were performed at a single concentration of 500 µg/mL. Anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, DPPH radical scavenging, and H 2 O 2 scavenging activities were assessed according to previously published protocols [ 31 , 33 – 35 ]. Results were expressed as percentage inhibition or scavenging relative to respective positive and negative controls. A fixed concentration was selected to enable comparative screening across treatments under uniform conditions.
As only one concentration was tested, direct IC 50 calculation was not feasible. The single concentration was chosen to provide a preliminary assessment of therapeutic potential and to compare effects with controls (AgNO 3 and standard drugs).
Justification for single concentration use In this study, a single concentration of 500 µg/mL was employed for all biomedical assays to provide an initial assessment of the biological potential of the biosynthesized silver nanoparticles. This approach allowed for efficient screening and proof-of-concept evaluation of their activity, conserving resources while confirming that the nanoparticles exhibit measurable effects. However, it is acknowledged as a limitation, as it does not allow determination of IC 50 values or a full dose–response profile. Future studies should include multiple concentrations to establish potency and therapeutic windows more accurately.
The anti-inflammatory properties of Ag–NPs were assessed following the protocols of [ 36 ] using a protein denaturation assay. Briefly, a working albumin solution was prepared by diluting 2 mL of 100 mg/10 mL PBS stock into 28 mL PBS. For each test sample, 300 µL of working albumin solution was mixed with 400 µL of Ag–NPs solution or Diclofenac sodium as a positive control. Vehicle control tubes contained 400 µL of DMSO. The mixtures were incubated at room temperature for 10 min, followed by heating at 65°C for 15 min to induce protein denaturation, and then cooled to room temperature. ### Macroscopic and microscopic morphological characterization of Musca domestica L.
The external morphology of Musca domestica L. was examined both macroscopically and microscopically to confirm specimen identity. As shown in Fig. 1 , “Panel a” (dorsal view) revealed large red compound eyes, short aristate antennae with prominent lateral bristles, and a gray thorax marked with four longitudinal black stripes. Wings were positioned dorsally, and the tarsus comprised five tarsomeres with a pretarsus terminating in two claws. “Panel b” (lateral view) showed a single pair of functional forewings that were transparent and membranous with distinct venation, characteristic of Diptera. Three pairs of segmented legs (forelegs, midlegs, and hindlegs) were attached ventrally, each consisting of a femur, tibia, tarsus, and pretarsus. “Panel c” (dorsal oblique view) highlighted well-defined red compound eyes, folded wings, a darkly pigmented thorax with four black longitudinal stripes, a yellowish-brown abdomen with visible segmental bands, and a proboscis extending ventrally from the head capsule [ 16 , 41 ].
Magnified macroscopic external morphological views of Musca domestica L. under natural light Microscopic examination (Fig. 2 ) further confirmed these traits. “Panel a” displayed the mouthparts, including a proboscis adapted for sucking and sponging, with sclerotized components (labrum, labium, maxillary palps). “Panel b” highlighted compound eye clusters with optic nerves. “Panel c” showed a transparent membranous wing with distinct venation and a dark oval pterostigma along the leading edge. “Panel d” revealed club-shaped halteres, modified hindwings acting as gyroscopic organs. “Panel e” depicted the hindleg, longer and more robust for propulsion, while “Panel f” illustrated the midleg, thicker and blunter, with a pretarsus bearing terminal claws.

### Verification of desired colour change at 70 °C
The initial qualitative assessment of Ag-NP formation relied on observable color changes, an established preliminary indicator of nanoparticle synthesis [ 23 ]. Upon addition of Musca domestica L. extract to a colorless silver nitrate solution and incubation at 70°C in a shaking water bath, the solution gradually changed to a red-brown hue, forming a distinct brown colloid within 15 min (Fig. 3 ). This visible transformation is attributed to the reduction of Ag + ions to metallic Ag 0 nanoparticles, corroborating the formation of Ag–NPs.

### UV–Vis spectroscopy analysis
The formation of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) was further confirmed by UV–Vis spectroscopy (Fig. 4 ). The observed SPR peak at 475 nm confirms the formation of Ag–NPs and falls within the typical range of 400–500 nm reported for green-synthesized silver nanoparticles [ 25 ]. This range is attributed to surface plasmon resonance (SPR), a phenomenon arising from the collective oscillation of conduction electrons at the interface between negatively charged electrons and the positively charged metal lattice upon interaction with incident light [ 25 ].

### Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) analysis
SEM was employed to directly visualize the morphology and size distribution of the synthesized Ag–NPs (Fig. 5 ). The images revealed predominantly spherical nanoparticles with diameters ranging approximately from 70 to 82 nm. The average particle size was determined to be 76 ± 6 nm. Similar findings have been reported in several studies, including a study conducted in 2024 [ 12 ]. This observed variation of 0.0058 is described here as “size distribution from SEM”, rather than polydispersity index (PDI), since PDI is conventionally derived from dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements [ 27 ].
SEM image showing the spherical shape and uniform size distribution of Ag–NPs The DLS analysis (Sect. 3.8 ) reported a hydrodynamic diameter of 258.5 nm with a PDI of 0.371. The larger DLS value compared to SEM is expected, as DLS measures the particle plus its surrounding hydration layer and any potential aggregation in solution, whereas SEM measures dry, individual nanoparticles. These differences highlight that the Ag–NPs, while relatively uniform in their intrinsic size, may form loose aggregates in suspension, contributing to the larger hydrodynamic diameter. Similar results were observed in a 2025 study [ 3 ].

### X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis
XRD analysis was conducted to evaluate the crystalline nature and phase purity of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs (Fig. 6 ). The diffraction pattern exhibited prominent peaks at 38.1° (111), 44.3° (200), 64.4° (220), and 77.3° (311), consistent with the face-centered cubic (fcc) structure of metallic silver [ 12 ]. These reflections confirm the formation of crystalline Ag–NPs at the nanoscale. The calculated average crystallite size, using the Debye–Scherrer equation, was approximately 9.72 nm, indicating nanocrystalline properties.

### Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
The EDX spectrum (Fig. 7 ) provided a detailed elemental composition of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs. A strong peak at 3 keV confirmed the presence of silver, which accounted for 20.01% of the total mass. The relatively low silver content, compared to theoretical 100% silver, reflects the presence of stabilizing biomolecules and other elements derived from the housefly extract [ 7 ]. These capping molecules, including proteins, sugars, and phenolics, coat the nanoparticle surface and are detected by EDX, reducing the apparent silver mass fraction.
EDX spectrum showing the elemental composition of Ag–NPs with a dominant silver peak Other elements detected included C, O, Na, Mg, Al, Ca, and Au. Carbon and oxygen are expected, as they arise from organic biomolecules present in the housefly extract. Sodium and magnesium may be derived from salts or mineral components within the extract. Trace amounts of aluminum, calcium, or gold could result from environmental exposure of the flies, sample preparation, or the substrate used for SEM imaging. These findings align with previous reports of biologically synthesized nanoparticles where non-metallic residues and elemental traces are commonly observed [ 13 ].

### Biomolecule Identification via Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis (Comparative study)
The FTIR spectrum of the Musca domestica L. extract revealed characteristic absorption bands corresponding to diverse biomolecular functional groups, which were also observed in the biosynthesized Ag–NPs spectrum with notable variations (Fig. 8 a and b), summarized in Table 3 . In the extract, a broad band in the range of 3700–3200 cm −1 is attributed to O–H stretching vibrations of hydroxyl groups present in phenolics, proteins, and carbohydrates. A less intense band in the 2800–2600 cm −1 region corresponds to C–H stretching vibrations of aliphatic chains in sugars and other organic molecules [ 1 ]. The band around 1651–1631 cm −1 is assigned to C=O stretching of carbonyl groups and aromatic structures [ 3 ], while the region between 1365 and 1030 cm −1 represents C–N, C–O, and C–O–C stretching vibrations, indicating the presence of amines, alcohols, ethers, and reducing sugars [ 30 ].
FTIR spectra of a biosynthesized Ag–NPs and b Musca domestica L. extract, showing functional group variations associated with nanoparticle formation In comparison, the biosynthesized Ag–NPs spectrum retained these functional group signatures but exhibited shifts in peak positions and changes in intensity, indicating interactions between silver ions and biomolecules during nanoparticle formation. The broad O–H/N–H band around 3273 cm −1 appeared more intense and slightly shifted, suggesting enhanced hydrogen bonding and possible involvement of hydroxyl- and amine-containing compounds in nanoparticle synthesis [ 3 ]. Such changes may also be influenced by environmental factors such as pH and local ionic conditions during synthesis, which can alter hydrogen bonding and biomolecular conformation.
The bands at 1637 cm −1 and 1344 cm −1 showed slight shifts relative to the extract, indicating potential interaction of carbonyl and aromatic groups with Ag + ions. These groups may contribute to electron transfer processes required for reduction, although this cannot be conclusively establish

### Zeta size and potential
The hydrodynamic size of the biosynthesized Ag–NPs was determined by dynamic light scattering (DLS) and found to be 258.5 nm, with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.371 (Fig. 9 a). This hydrodynamic size is substantially larger than the size observed in SEM analysis (76 ± 6 nm), which represents the core metallic nanoparticles [ 43 ]. Similar findings have been reported in the literature, with [ 28 ] determining the average hydrodynamic size of Ag–NPs to be 231.8 nm. The discrepancy arises because DLS measures the effective diameter of particles in suspension, including the hydration layer and any adsorbed biomolecules from the housefly extract that act as capping agents. Furthermore, partial aggregation in aqueous media can contribute to a larger observed size in DLS measurements.
a Zeta size distribution of Ag–NPs synthesized using housefly extract, showing an average hydrodynamic size of 258.5 nm with a PDI of 0.371. b Zeta potential distribution indicating a surface charge of − 7.98 ± 5.93 mV The PDI of 0.371, while below 0.5, indicates moderate polydispersity, reflecting some size variation in the colloidal suspension [ 22 , 44 ]. In comparison, the “size distribution from SEM” suggests relatively uniform individual nanoparticles but does not account for the surrounding hydration layer or aggregation in solution. This comparison emphasizes the importance of using both imaging and hydrodynamic measurements to fully characterize nanoparticle populations.
The zeta potential of the Ag–NPs was measured at − 7.98 mV (Fig. 9 b). Although a negative value suggests some degree of electrostatic repulsion, it is relatively low compared to the ± 30 mV threshold typically considered necessary for long-term colloidal stability [ 44 ]. Therefore, the nanoparticles may possess moderate short-term stability, sufficient for the current in vitro assays, but might be prone to aggregation over extended storage or under varying physicochemical conditions. ### Therapeutic potential of biosynthesized Ag–NPs
The therapeutic potential of biosynthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) was systematically evaluated through in vitro assays, including anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, and antioxidant activities. Percentage inhibition values were calculated from triplicate (n = 3) absorbance measurements.
In the anti-inflammatory assay, Ag–NPs showed moderate inhibition of protein denaturation (21.73% ± 1.55% b ) relative to AgNO 3 (9.54% ± 1.35% c ) and the housefly extract (5.01% ± 0.85% d ), whereas Diclofenac, used as a standard, displayed the highest inhibition (36.04% ± 1.93% a ) (Table 4 ). DMSO, serving as a negative control, showed negligible activity (0.00% e ). One-way ANOVA indicated significant differences among treatments (F 4,10 = 80.58, p &lt; 0.001), and Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis confirmed that Ag–NPs’ activity was significantly greater than both AgNO 3 and the extract, but lower than Diclofenac (p &lt; 0.05). These results highlight the enhanced anti-inflammatory potential of Ag–NPs compared to ionic silver and the crude extract, likely due to nanoparticle-mediated stabilization and bioactive surface functionalization [ 9 , 33 ].
In vitro biological activities of biosynthesized Ag–NPs compared with AgNO 3 , extract, and standard controls. Values represent mean ± SD (n = 3). Different superscript letters indicate significant differences (Tukey HSD, p &lt; 0.05)
Superscripts (a–e) indicate statistically significant differences between treatments ( p &lt; 0.05) as determined by Tukey’s post hoc test For anti-diabetic activity, evaluated via α-amylase inhibition, Ag–NPs exhibited 36.76% ± 0.97% b inhibition, slightly higher than AgNO 3 (34.99% ± 0.68% b ) and significantly higher than the extract (2.57% ± 0.60% c ) and DMSO (0.00% c ). Glucophage, the standard drug, showed the highest inhibition (62.04% ± 1.06%^a^) (Table 1 ). ### Discussion
The biosynthesis of Ag–NPs using Musca domestica L. extract represents a complex biologically mediated redox system in which diverse insect-derived metabolites collectively govern nanoparticle formation and stabilization.
The UV–Vis spectral analysis further confirms nanoparticle formation, with an SPR peak observed at 475 nm within the typical range of 400–500 nm for green-synthesized Ag–NPs [ 25 ]. Comparable studies have reported SPR peaks at 463 nm ( Justicia adhatoda ), 488 nm ( Equisetum arvense ), and 445 nm ( Withania coagulans ), indicating that the optical response is strongly influenced by the biological source [ 25 ]. The slight red-shift observed in the present study may be attributed to biomolecule-induced changes in the local dielectric environment and mild interparticle interactions, which increase the effective particle size [ 32 ]. These findings emphasize that nanoparticle optical properties are governed not only by size but also by interfacial chemistry and surface-bound organic layers [ 34 , 46 ]. The physicochemical characteristics, including moderate dispersity (PDI = 0.385) and the discrepancy between primary particle size and hydrodynamic diameter, indicate the formation of a biomolecular corona and soft agglomeration in aqueous environments [ 3 ]. Such behavior is widely reported in green-synthesized nanoparticles and is attributed to the adsorption of organic constituents rather than actual particle growth [ 37 ]. This suggests that the nanoparticles exist as hybrid organic–inorganic systems, where surface-bound biomolecules significantly influence colloidal behavior and functionality.
The colloidal stability of the synthesized nanoparticles appears to be primarily governed by steric rather than electrostatic effects. The relatively low zeta potential, together with the increased hydrodynamic size, suggests that stabilization is achieved through a biomolecular coating that limits aggregation via physical hindrance [ 15 , 37 ]. ### Limitations of the study
While this work establishes the feasibility of using M. domestica aqueous extract for Ag–NP biosynthesis, several limitations exist:
Exploratory Design and Random Sampling Flies were collected randomly from markets without controlling for gender or age. This may introduce variability in biochemical composition. Future studies should employ lab-reared flies to standardize the extract.
Single-Concentration Bioassays In vitro assays were conducted at a single concentration, preventing IC 50 determination. Although preliminary bioactivity was demonstrated, future studies should include dose–response analyses to calculate IC 50 and fully quantify therapeutic potential.
Comparison with Solvent-Based Extracts While prior studies used ethanolic or methanolic extracts, the current work employed aqueous extraction for environmental and biocompatibility reasons. Direct side-by-side experimental comparisons with solvent-based extracts could strengthen conclusions regarding efficiency and functional equivalence.
Optimization of Synthesis Parameters Temperature and incubation time were selected based on preliminary observations, not a full factorial optimization. Future work should systematically evaluate parameters such as pH, temperature, extract-to-silver ratio, and incubation duration to refine synthesis efficiency and nanoparticle stability.
Biochemical Variability Variations in metabolite composition of houseflies may affect reproducibility. Comprehensive profiling of bioactive compounds in the extract could provide mechanistic insights and enhance consistency.

### Future directions and recommendations
Future investigations should aim for a more detailed mechanistic understanding of nanoparticle formation by isolating and characterizing the specific biomolecular fractions responsible for reduction and capping. While the present findings suggest a synergistic role of proteins, phenolics, and other metabolites, the relative contribution of each component remains unclear. Advanced analytical approaches, such as proteomic and metabolomic profiling, could identify key functional molecules and elucidate their binding interactions with metal ions, enabling more controlled and reproducible synthesis pathways.
To strengthen the biological interpretation of these findings, systematic dose–response evaluations are necessary to determine IC 50 values and establish concentration-dependent effects. This would facilitate rigorous comparison with existing nanomaterials and conventional agents, while clarifying whether observed activities are primarily nanoparticle-driven or influenced by residual ionic silver or surface-associated biomolecules.
Standardization of the biological source represents another critical requirement. Variations in metabolite composition due to age, diet, or physiological state of Musca domestica L. may significantly influence nanoparticle characteristics. The use of controlled, lab-reared specimens under defined conditions could minimize batch-to-batch variability and enhance reproducibility, a recognized limitation in bio-mediated synthesis systems.
Further studies should include cytotoxicity and biocompatibility assessments using relevant mammalian cell models to define safety profiles, which is essential if the biomedical potential of these nanoparticles is to be claimed. In parallel, stability optimization through surface engineering, such as controlled functionalization or selective purification of capping layers, may improve colloidal stability and enable more predictable interactions in biological environments.

### Conclusion
Silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) were successfully synthesized using houseflies extract as a novel bioresource via a rapid and green approach. The present study demonstrates that Musca domestica L. extract can serve as a novel and effective bioresource for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs). The nanoparticles exhibit well-defined crystalline structures, moderate colloidal stability, and surface functionalization by biomolecules, as confirmed through UV–Vis, SEM, FTIR, Zeta Potential. DLS, and XRD analyses. Mechanistic insights suggest that proteins, phenolics, and other metabolites act synergistically to reduce Ag + ions and stabilize the resulting nanoparticles, while FTIR-identified functional groups provide molecular-level justification for their potent antioxidant activity.
Functionally, the biosynthesized Ag–NPs exhibit promising anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-diabetic activities. Although ionic silver contributes to some observed effects, the surface-bound biomolecules and nanoparticle interface likely enhance overall performance, highlighting the importance of hybrid organic–inorganic structures. These findings underscore the potential of insect-mediated nanoparticle synthesis as a sustainable and versatile platform for biomedical applications.

### Background
In recent decades, nanoparticles (NPs) have emerged as a subject of immense importance across multiple scientific disciplines. Their applications have proliferated in various industries, including pharmaceuticals, medicine, cosmetics, construction, and electronics, making them integral to materials science [ 1 ]. The growing interest in nanoparticles is driven by their unique properties and potential for innovative applications in these fields. Nanoparticles are distinguished by their nanoscale size, typically ranging from 1 to 100 nm, which results in a high surface area-to-volume ratio, enhanced surface reactivity, and unique physicochemical properties. They also exhibit diverse morphologies, including nanotubes, nanorods, nanoconjugates, and nanowires, which differ significantly from their bulk counterparts [ 1 ].
Furthermore, metal NPs have garnered widespread attention owing to their unique properties, including anticancer, antimicrobial, and antioxidant activities, as well as distinctive physicochemical characteristics such as controlled morphology, conductivity, particle size distribution, and optical and magnetic properties [ 2 , 3 ]. Although various methods exist for synthesizing NPs, physical and chemical approaches are recognized for their energy-intensive nature, environmental toxicity, and high cost. In contrast, biosynthesis, often referred to as "green synthesis," offers an eco-friendly alternative that requires lower energy consumption and financial investment, resulting in biocompatible nanoparticles [ 4 ]. Biosynthesis employs a range of biological sources, such as plants, microbes, and algae, to produce metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional synthesis methods [ 5 ].

### Research gap
Traditionally, the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (Ag–NPs) has predominantly relied on plant and microbial bioresources. Plant-mediated approaches have utilized species such as Moringa oleifera , Azadirachta indica (Neem), Bryophyllum pinnatum , and Citrullus colocynthis , where metabolites including flavonoids, tannins, and proteins act as reducing and stabilizing agents [ 2 , 14 , 15 ]. Microbial systems, including fungi and bacteria, have also been explored for biogenic Ag-NP production, though these processes often require longer incubation periods, precise culture conditions, and post-culture processing [ 16 ].
In contrast, the use of animal-derived systems, particularly insects, remains underexplored despite their rich biochemical composition. Musca domestica L. (housefly) was selected in this study based on several practical and mechanistic considerations: its global abundance and ease of collection, minimal maintenance requirements, and the presence of diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and metabolites, capable of reducing Ag + ions and stabilizing nanoparticles [ 15 , 17 – 19 ]. The use of whole insect extract provides a complex biochemical environment that supports rapid nanoparticle formation (within 15 min) without the need for additional chemicals, highlighting a chemical-free and efficient synthesis approach.

### Experimental design, and laboratory setting
The experimental workflow comprised several sequential stages: (i) collection and taxonomic verification of houseflies, (ii) preparation of aqueous extract, (iii) biosynthesis of Ag–NPs, (iv) detailed physicochemical characterization including UV–Vis spectroscopy, FTIR, SEM, EDX, XRD, DLS, and zeta potential analysis, and (v) in vitro assessment of therapeutic potential. Each step was designed to ensure reproducibility and reliability, with triplicate measurements, multiple runs, and standardized protocols applied throughout. Statistical analysis is conducted to determine significance, compare groups, and interpret data. Laboratory setting

### Collection &amp; extract preparation of houseflies
Following a modified protocol by Jakinala et al. [ 21 ], 300 adult houseflies ( Musca domestica L.) were collected randomly in polythene bags from meat, fruit, and vegetable markets in Karachi. This exploratory approach was intended to assess the practical potential of M. domestica extract without introducing bias from laboratory-reared specimens or chemical additives. Flies were euthanized via asphyxiation, and a subset of 30 specimens was sent to the Department of Zoology, University of Karachi, for taxonomic verification. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed the species identity.
The collected flies were washed three times with ethanol and deionized water to remove surface contaminants. To preserve the natural biochemical composition, no organic solvent-based extraction (ethanol or methanol) was performed. The flies were then homogenized in deionized water, filtered through the exoskeleton using a sieve, and centrifuged at 7000 rpm for 20 min. The resulting supernatant was collected and stored at 4°C for subsequent silver nanoparticle synthesis and in vitro analyses [ 21 , 22 ].
As this study was exploratory, flies were collected randomly without controlling for gender or developmental stage. While this introduces natural variability in metabolite composition, it reflects real-world conditions and allows a practical evaluation of the extract’s utility. Future studies may employ laboratory-reared flies of defined age and gender to standardize metabolite profiles, optimize nanoparticle synthesis, and enhance reproducibility and mechanistic understanding.

### Biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles
The biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles was carried out by mixing the prepared housefly extract with a 1 mM aqueous solution of silver nitrate (AgNO 3 ) at a ratio of 1:9 (extract: AgNO 3 ). A control sample, containing distilled water instead of the extract, was prepared to account for any non-biological reduction of silver ions. The mixture was incubated in a shaking water bath at 70°C for 15 min [ 25 ]. The selected temperature and incubation time were based on preliminary optimization trials, which indicated that these conditions promoted efficient reduction of Ag + ions, as evidenced by a rapid and stable color change from colorless to reddish-brown, without compromising the stability or uniformity of the nanoparticles. The formation of Ag–NPs under these conditions is consistent with previously reported green synthesis protocols, where moderate heat accelerates the bioreduction process without denaturing the bioactive compounds in the extract [ 21 , 22 , 26 ].
Following incubation, the colloidal suspension was visually monitored for the characteristic reddish-brown color, indicating successful nanoparticle formation. The resulting Ag–NPs were stored at 4°C until further physicochemical characterization and in vitro biochemical analyses. This approach ensures reproducibility, as the standardized temperature and time conditions consistently yielded nanoparticles of comparable size and stability across replicate preparations as demonstrated in Tables 1 and 2 . The method reflects an eco-friendly and practical synthesis strategy while minimizing the need for hazardous chemicals.

### Characterization of biogenic nanoparticles
Visual investigation of nanoparticles
Formation of Ag–NPs was first confirmed visually, followed by quantitative UV–Vis spectroscopy using a BIOBASE BK-S360 spectrophotometer over 300–600 nm. Measurements were performed in triplicate across multiple days to ensure reproducibility [ 21 , 22 , 25 ]. A summary of UV–Vis absorbance runs and replicates is provided in Table 1 . Morphological analysis (SEM)
A drop of the colloidal suspension was deposited on a glass coverslip, air-dried, and observed under SEM (JSM-6380) at 35,000 × magnification [ 3 , 12 ]. Particle shapes and sizes were determined, and size distribution was calculated as σ/μ, providing insight into homogeneity [ 27 ]. To avoid confusion with DLS polydispersity index (PDI), this is reported as “size distribution from SEM.” Structural analysis (XRD)
Dried Ag-NP powder was analyzed using a Bruker D2 Phaser XRD system with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å) in Bragg–Brentano geometry (2θ = 10–80°, 1°/min). Crystal planes were assigned using JCPDS Card No. 04-0783. Crystallite sizes were calculated using the Scherrer equation [ 26 ].
where D = crystallite size, K = 0.9, λ = 1.54 nm, β = FWHM in radians, θ = Bragg angle. For the most intense peak observed at approximately 38.35° (111), the FWHM (β) was 0.151 rad. Elemental analysis (EDX)
EDX was performed on SEM-mounted samples over 0–20 keV to determine elemental composition and assess potential contaminants [ 28 ]. FTIR analysis
FTIR spectra were recorded to identify functional groups responsible for Ag + reduction and nanoparticle stabilization. Sixteen scans with a resolution of 4 cm −1 were collected over 4000–400 cm −1 [ 25 , 29 ]. A summary table of major peaks and probable functional groups is provided in Table 3 .

### In Vitro biological evaluations of biosynthesized Ag–NPs
All assays were performed at a single concentration of 500 µg/mL. Anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, DPPH radical scavenging, and H 2 O 2 scavenging activities were assessed according to previously published protocols [ 31 , 33 – 35 ]. Results were expressed as percentage inhibition or scavenging relative to respective positive and negative controls. A fixed concentration was selected to enable comparative screening across treatments under uniform conditions.
As only one concentration was tested, direct IC 50 calculation was not feasible. The single concentration was chosen to provide a preliminary assessment of therapeutic potential and to compare effects with controls (AgNO 3 and standard drugs).
Justification for single concentration use In this study, a single concentration of 500 µg/mL was employed for all biomedical assays to provide an initial assessment of the biological potential of the biosynthesized silver nanoparticles. This approach allowed for efficient screening and proof-of-concept evaluation of their activity, conserving resources while confirming that the nanoparticles exhibit measurable effects. However, it is acknowledged as a limitation, as it does not allow determination of IC 50 values or a full dose–response profile. Future studies should include multiple concentrations to establish potency and therapeutic windows more accurately.
The anti-inflammatory properties of Ag–NPs were assessed following the protocols of [ 36 ] using a protein denaturation assay. Briefly, a working albumin solution was prepared by diluting 2 mL of 100 mg/10 mL PBS stock into 28 mL PBS. For each test sample, 300 µL of working albumin solution was mixed with 400 µL of Ag–NPs solution or Diclofenac sodium as a positive control. Vehicle control tubes contained 400 µL of DMSO. The mixtures were incubated at room temperature for 10 min, followed by heating at 65°C for 15 min to induce protein denaturation, and then cooled to room temperature.
